name: Face tape / sleep patches for wrinkles

image.caption: A face made of tape on an enclosure by Alexander Plyushchev - IMG 1490

lead: Face tape and sleep patches are adhesive strips or silicone and hydrocolloid-style pads stuck on the forehead, between the brows, around the eyes or near the mouth before bed. People wear them to smooth existing lines and stop new creases from forming overnight.

The idea is that holding skin flat and covered reduces creasing from facial movement and pillow pressure; occlusion is known to reduce water loss from skin. Claims rest mainly on manufacturer marketing and user testimonials, and no published clinical trials for wrinkles were found. Treatments with an established research base, such as botulinum toxin for frown lines and prescription retinoids, are different products.

paras: Users apply the patch to clean, dry skin as the last step of a night routine and remove it in the morning, often after a serum or moisturiser. People commonly combine it with back-sleeping and retinoids, and judge it over weeks.
Adhesives can cause irritation or contact dermatitis in some people. They are sold as cosmetics, not as approved wrinkle treatments. Sensitive or broken skin is a common reason to avoid adhesives.

angle.text: Users stick tape or silicone patches on the forehead, brows and eyes before bed so skin stays flat overnight, aiming for smoother lines and fewer new creases. They are sold as cosmetics, and trials on wrinkles were not found.

lead: Face tape and sleep patches are adhesive strips or silicone and hydrocolloid-style pads that people stick on the forehead, between the brows, around the eyes or on the mouth area before bed, with the aim of flattening or preventing lines that form from facial expression or sleeping position. They are sold as cosmetic products and are not medical devices with a recognised wrinkle indication.

Wrinkles are generally attributed to a mix of repeated facial movement, ageing, sun exposure, smoking, low hydration and habitual sleeping position.[1] Treatments with an established evidence base are different in kind: botulinum toxin, which is FDA-approved for glabellar (frown) lines, and the prescription retinoids tretinoin and tazarotene.[1] Wikipedia's wrinkle article does not mention tape or patches.[1]

No published clinical trials of face tape or sleep patches for wrinkles were located in the sources reviewed for this article. Claims about them rest mainly on manufacturer marketing and user testimonials.
infobox: Overnight, on forehead, brows, eyes or mouth area

paras: Products include thin flexible tape cut into strips, silicone sheets reusable across several nights, and hydrocolloid or hydrogel patches that sit on the skin. Some carry added ingredients such as peptides or hyaluronic acid, which fall into the glycosaminoglycan and hydration-product category that Wikipedia describes as offering temporary support for hydration.[1]

Proponents say that keeping the skin physically held flat limits creasing from repeated expression or from pressing the face into a pillow, and that occlusion keeps the area moist. Habitual sleeping position is listed among recognised contributors to wrinkles.[1] Occlusive films in general are known to slow water loss from skin.[2] Whether tape alters wrinkle depth over time has not been tested in a published trial.

Adhesives can cause contact dermatitis or irritation in some users; moisturisers and skin-contact products in general are documented causes of contact dermatitis.[2] Dermatologists commonly caution that sensitive or broken skin may react to adhesives, but no study specific to these products was identified.
